metadata.title: Code That Fits in Your Head: Heuristics for Software Engineering
metadata.author: Mark Seemann

system_instruction:
You are applying Mark Seemann's cognitive-load principles to real work.

**How to use this JSON:**
1. Identify which principle applies to your situation
2. Read the principle's statement and tags
3. Review supporting_arguments for evidence and reasoning
4. Check related_implications for practical application
5. Consult related_questions to probe deeper

**RULES:**
- Only cite what's in this JSON
- Quote supporting_arguments when making claims
- Use source references to trace arguments back to the book
- If a principle doesn't apply, say so clearly
- If you need anti-patterns or checklists, acknowledge they're not in this data

Everything here is sourced directly from the book. Nothing is invented.

principles.statement: Use heuristics (guidelines based on experience) rather than absolute rules. Rules create false confidence; heuristics require judgment and understanding of context.

supporting_arguments.name: Legacy Code Exponential Cost Growth
supporting_arguments.claim: Each new feature in old code requires more time to understand and modify, due to exponential complexity growth.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Version 1: add feature in 1 day. Version 5: same feature takes 2 days (understand existing code). Version 10: same feature takes 1 week (too many dependencies). Initial design was simple; each feature was 'glued' to existing architecture; at critical complexity, any change requires refactoring half the system. Cognitive load grows exponentially not linearly; complexity curve starts flat then spikes sharply.

related_implications.name: Limit Function and Module Size
related_implications.what_means: Rule 80/24: function max 80 characters wide, 24 lines tall (fits on screen without scroll). Cyclomatic complexity: <5 very simple, 5-10 moderate, >15 too complex. Refactor if exceeds limits.
related_implications.when_applies: Every code review. When writing functions.
related_implications.why_matters: Limits are heuristics (not absolute rules) but prevent cognitive overload. Enforces thinking in smaller pieces.

related_questions.text: How do heuristics differ from absolute rules?

principles.statement: Developer spends 90% of time reading and understanding code, 10% writing. Optimize for readability not speed.

supporting_arguments.name: Code That Fits Reduces Errors 10x
supporting_arguments.claim: If function/module is understandable whole, errors decrease dramatically.
supporting_arguments.evidence: When reading understandable code, developer builds complete mental model. When reading complex code, brain overloads, attention jumps around, misses details → errors. Empirical: cyclomatic complexity <5 almost no errors; 5-10 errors visible in review; >15 each change introduces new bugs.

related_implications.name: Write Integration Test Before Code
related_implications.what_means: Before developing feature, write integration test showing usage. Test won't compile (no code yet), but you design API through usage not fantasy. If test is hard to write, API is bad.
related_implications.when_applies: Before every feature. When designing APIs.
related_implications.why_matters: API born from usage → usable. Better design emerges.

related_questions.text: How does asymmetry between reading and writing affect design?

principles.statement: Human brain holds ~7-9 concepts in working memory. Functions requiring 50 concepts are the enemy. 20 small functions better than 1 large complex.

supporting_arguments.name: Readable Code Reduces Errors
supporting_arguments.claim: Understanding code reduces errors by 10x+ because mental model is complete.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Complex code → brain overloaded → attention jumps → misses details → errors. Simplicity → complete model → fewer errors.

related_implications.name: Create Checklist for New Codebase
related_implications.what_means: Before business logic: (1) Git init, (2) .gitignore configured, (3) Build automated, (4) Compiler warns on ALL, (5) Static analysis ON, (6) Unit tests ready, (7) CI/CD pipeline created.
related_implications.why_matters: If added later, 10x harder. Saves hours debugging 'works on my machine'.

related_questions.text: What is cognitive load and why does it matter?

principles.statement: Encapsulation is not 'hide private' but protecting immutable properties (invariants) that are always true.

supporting_arguments.name: Encapsulation as Contract Between Code and Reader
supporting_arguments.claim: When class protects invariants, reader can rely on guarantees without checking everywhere.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Example Money class: Bad—Amount public, can be negative; Currency can be null. Good—private fields, constructor validates, properties readonly. Reader: 'Money never has negative amount' guaranteed. No need `if (money.Amount >= 0)` everywhere.

related_implications.name: Encapsulate Data, Protect Invariants
related_implications.what_means: When creating class, ask: 'What properties must ALWAYS be true?' Example: Reservation name required (not null), partySize 1-20, date not past. Protect in constructor with validation. Properties readonly.
related_implications.why_matters: Reader knows object is always valid. Reduces cognitive load (no need defensive checks).

related_questions.text: What are invariants and why protect them?

principles.statement: Break large functions into small ones not for 'rules' but so reader understands each piece separately.

supporting_arguments.name: Code Comprehension Benefits of Simplicity
supporting_arguments.claim: Small understandable units reduce errors via complete mental models.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Complexity <5 no errors; 5-10 some errors; >15 always bugs.

related_implications.name: Complexity Limits
related_implications.what_means: 80/24 rule: function must fit on screen. Cyclomatic complexity <10. Use tools to measure. Enforce in CI/CD.

related_questions.text: How does function size affect understanding?

principles.statement: Develop full feature end-to-end (vertical slice) not layer-by-layer. Reveals design errors early.

supporting_arguments.name: Vertical Slice Reveals Design Errors Early
supporting_arguments.claim: Layer-by-layer approach reveals problems at month 3; vertical slices reveal at day 1.
supporting_arguments.evidence: Layered bad: Month 1 models, Month 2 controllers, Month 3 realize they don't fit. Vertical good: Day 1 full feature works, team sees design, discusses, expands. Errors caught day 1 not month 3.

related_implications.name: Integration Test Guides Design
related_implications.what_means: Write end-to-end test first (HTTP to database). Show how code should be used. Test can't compile (no code). You write minimal code for compilation. Test fails (no implementation). You implement. Test passes. API designed through usage.
related_implications.why_matters: API usable because born from usage.

related_questions.text: Why develop vertically instead of by layers?

principles.statement: Write integration test (how used), then unit tests (details), then code. API designed from usage perspective.

supporting_arguments.name: Outside-In Testing Produces Better API
supporting_arguments.claim: Testing from outside (how code is used) produces better API design than inside-out (code first).
supporting_arguments.evidence: Integration test written first shows intended usage. If test is hard to write, API is bad (feedback). API emerges usable from perspective of caller not implementer.

related_implications.name: Test Structure: Arrange-Act-Assert
related_implications.what_means: Every test: Arrange (setup data), Act (perform action), Assert (verify). Use comments // Arrange, // Act, // Assert.
related_implications.why_matters: Clear structure. Easy to follow. New devs learn pattern.

related_questions.text: Why test outside-in instead of inside-out?

principles.statement: Checklists convert knowledge (in head) into action (in Git). Like pilot's preflight check: prevents human memory failure.

supporting_arguments.name: Checklists Work Because They Convert Knowledge to Action
supporting_arguments.claim: Expert pilot doesn't 'remember' checklist during flight—executes automatically. Saves in critical moments. Human memory unreliable.
supporting_arguments.evidence: B-17 airplane 1930s: so complex pilots often crashed despite working aircraft. Engineers created preflight checklist. Errors dropped 90%. Applied to code: commit checklist (run tests? format?), code-review checklist (edge cases? good names?), new codebase checklist (Git? compiler warnings? CI/CD?).

related_implications.name: Codebase Setup Checklist
related_implications.what_means: Before writing business logic: Git init, .gitignore, automated build, compiler warnings ALL ON, static analysis ON, unit tests, CI/CD pipeline ready.
related_implications.why_matters: If added later: 10x harder. Now: foundation ready.

related_questions.text: How do checklists improve code quality?
